newsitem.title: GERMANY: German notables rally to cause of Bosnian refugees.
newsitem.headline: German notables rally to cause of Bosnian refugees.

text.p: Leading German public figures, including former foreign minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher, made a public appeal on Friday for changes to the practice of forcibly repatriating Bosnian refugees.

The signatories of the appeal, addressed to Interior Minister Manfred Kanther and his regional state counterparts, said the current practice could lead to increased tension in Bosnia and was damaging Germany's international image.

"As soon as peace becomes reality in Bosnia, tens of thousands of Bosnians will return home voluntarily," the appeal said. "Those who know the situation also know that the state of peace has not yet been achieved in Bosnia."

The text was also signed by Ignatz Bubis, the leader of Germany's Jewish community, Bosnia mediator Christian Schwarz-Schilling and Hans Koschnick, the former European Union administrator of the Bosnian city of Mostar.
They singled out the deportation earlier this week of a group of Bosnian refugees from Berlin and Bavaria for criticism.
"Among those deported were pregnant women, patients receiving treatment for heart illness and other people whose deportation is incomprehensibe," the signatories said.
They also said Germany was deporting refugees back to the Bosnian Serb entity, Republika Srpska, which they described as being "controlled by radical forces".
Even refugees from Srebrenica, the Moslem enclave overrun in 1995 by Serbs who expelled some 40,000 people and where 8,000 men remain unaccounted for, were being sent home, they said.
"This is overstepping a boundary correctly drawn by post-war Germany, with its commitment to human rights," the appeal said.

"The current examples of the deportation practice allow the conclusion to be drawn that the wellbeing of those returning and Germany's international interests are not being observed sufficiently, or not being observed at all."

Germany took in more than 300,000 Bosnian refugees -- more than the rest of the European Union put together. Kanther and regional interior ministers agreed last year the refugees could be forcibly reptatriated if they refused to go home.
Conservative-ruled regional states have already carried out the practice but others have not resorted to it so far.
